prompt.context: The beverage department of a regional supermarket has seen a drop in revenue over the last year and has hired your firm to determine the cause of the decline and recommend ways to reverse the trend.
prompt.question: What is causing the revenue decline in the beverage department, and what would you recommend to reverse the trend?

clarifying_info.a: The client is a leading regional grocer within the southeastern U.S.
The competitive landscape has not changed in the last year.

clarifying_info.q: Is the revenue decline across the whole store or just beverages?
clarifying_info.a: The revenue decline is specifically within the beverage segment.

clarifying_info.q: What does the client ultimately want from us?
clarifying_info.a: The client wants to find the cause of the declining revenue and recommendations for how to stop the decline.

exhibits.title: Revenues and Costs by Beverage Category
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down gallons sold (MM, average per store) and price per gallon ($) and cost per gallon ($) for three beverage categories — Sodas, Waters, and Others — across 2014 and 2015.

exhibits.title: Sodas by Brand
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down gallons sold (MM, average per store) and revenue ($M, average per store) for three soda brands — Brand A, Brand B, and Value Brand — across 2014 and 2015.

framework: Focus on revenue levers: price × volume (quantity), separated by beverage category
Segment revenue by category (Sodas, Waters, Others) to isolate where the decline is occurring
Drill down into the declining category by sub-segment (soda brands) to identify the specific driver
Apply 4P's framework (Price, Promotion, Product, Placement) to generate recommendations for reversing the decline
Avoid cost analysis — the prompt is revenue-focused

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate total revenue for each beverage category in 2014 and 2015. Which category is driving the overall decline?
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply gallons × price per gallon for each category in each year. The key insight is that only Sodas show a decline; Waters and Others are flat or growing. This should drive the candidate to ask for further segmentation of soda revenue.

math.answer: Revenue decline is entirely driven by Sodas (−$6M), partially offset by small gains in Waters (+$0.3M) and Others (+$1M).

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the implied price per gallon for each soda brand in 2014 and 2015. What is driving the soda revenue decline?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute implied price = Revenue / Gallons for each brand. Brand A and Brand B prices are stable at $1/gallon. The Value Brand price dropped sharply from $0.60 to $0.40, even as its volume tripled. The combination of a deep price cut on the Value Brand and volume shift away from Brand A is the root cause of the soda decline.

steps: Brand A 2015: $30M / 30MM gal = $1.00/gal  →  No price change; volume down 20MM gal, revenue −$20M
Brand B 2015: $30M / 30MM gal = $1.00/gal  →  No price change; volume up 5MM gal, revenue +$5M
Value Brand 2015: $24M / 60MM gal = $0.40/gal  →  Price dropped $0.20; volume up 35MM gal, revenue +$9M
Net soda revenue change: −$20M (Brand A) + $5M (Brand B) + $9M (Value Brand) = −$6M
math.answer: The Value Brand's price dropped 33% (from $0.60 to $0.40/gal), which cannibalized Brand A volume. Despite tripling in volume, Value Brand revenue only increased $9M, insufficient to offset Brand A's $20M loss. Root cause: aggressive Value Brand pricing is eroding total soda revenue.

brainstorming.prompt: The client would like to hear your recommendations for how to reverse the decline in revenue of the beverage segment.

categories.name: Price
ideas: Raise the Value Brand price back toward $0.50–$0.60/gal to restore margin and reduce cannibalization of Brand A
Test price elasticity of Value Brand with incremental price increases
Review Brand A and Brand B pricing for promotional opportunities to regain lost volume

categories.name: Promotion
ideas: Run targeted promotions on Brand A to recover volume lost to Value Brand
Bundle premium brands with complementary products (e.g., snacks) to drive value perception
Use loyalty program data to re-engage former Brand A buyers

categories.name: Product
ideas: Introduce new SKUs or flavors for Brand A to differentiate from Value Brand
Improve Value Brand packaging/quality to justify a higher price point
Evaluate whether private-label / Value Brand serves a genuinely distinct consumer segment

categories.name: Placement
ideas: Review shelf placement — consider giving Brand A and Brand B more prominent shelf space vs. Value Brand
Reduce Value Brand facings to limit impulse substitution
Explore end-cap or checkout placement for premium brands

recommendation: Raise the price of the Value Brand to reduce cannibalization of Brand A revenue; the current pricing gap ($0.40 vs. $1.00) is too wide and is driving volume substitution that destroys total revenue
Improve differentiation between Brand A / Brand B and the Value Brand through packaging, placement, and promotions so consumers perceive sufficient quality premium to justify the price difference
risks: Raising Value Brand price may alienate price-sensitive customers who have switched to it, potentially losing volume without recovering Brand A sales
Aggressive pricing or promotional changes to Brand A or Brand B could strain supplier relationships
next_steps: Conduct price elasticity analysis for Value Brand to determine optimal price point
Explore bundling opportunities to increase sales of premium brands
Design marketing and in-store activities to differentiate Value Brand from Brand A and Brand B
Review shelf placement of Value Brand relative to premium brands to manage substitution
